verdict: No: the spec makes sure nothing sandbox-only is lost, but it never tells the owner what is stored where, who can read it, or how to export it, delete it or leave; the largest gap is that there is no inventory of stores and no leaving journey, while the tool is forbidden to delete and the owner is given no supported way to.

findings.defect: No single table lists every store the product writes or causes to exist with its owner, mode, readers and lifetime; the facts are spread over 01 1.1, 01 1.2, 02 2.3, 02 2.4, 02 2.5, 06 6.2 and 13 13.1, and some stores (sbx per-name volumes, refs in host clones, the state attic) appear in none as a store.
findings.scenario: An employer's security review asks a developer to list every place the tool keeps the employer's code, secrets and transcripts; the developer has to read seven sections and still misses the workload volumes and the ledger under $XDG_STATE_HOME, and answers wrongly.
findings.change: Add a section to 01 (beside 1.2), 'Where data lives', with one row per store: path; what goes in; whose data it is (the owner's notes, the employer's code, a tool cache, a trust record); mode; who can read it (host user, other local users, which sandbox mounts it); lifetime; and what rm, retire and leaving do to it. Rows: host tree, memory (entries, handoff, snapshot, salvage, import), .attic, review checkouts, host settings, host state and state attic, the ledger, spool, view, refs in romeu namespaces in host clones, sbx sandboxes and their per-name volumes, keychain entries named in settings, the signing agent socket. Generate a reference page from it (12 12.3) and link it from 02 2.3 and 02 2.4.
findings.cost: One table of about 15 rows and a generator row; a decision on the lifetime column, which findings L16-3 and L16-7 need anyway.

findings.defect: No journey, success criterion or guide shows that a user can stop using romeu and julieta and keep every clone as a plain clone and every note as plain files, so the clean-exit promise of 00 0.1 and 08 8.1 is never tested or documented.
findings.scenario: A user drops the product and deletes $HOME/dev to clean up, losing memory and unpushed salvage payloads; another user removes the binaries and leaves sandboxes, egress rules, volumes, refs/romeu/* in every clone and the ledger behind, with no idea they exist.
findings.change: Add J14 'Stop using romeu and julieta' to 09: push or recover unpushed work (J10 step 3); retire each project, or rm it; list what stays on purpose (host clones, memory as plain Markdown, .attic); then what the operator removes by hand and how: host settings, host state, the ledger, sbx sandboxes and volumes, romeu-applied egress rules, refs under refs/romeu/ and refs/sandboxes/ (with the git command), keychain entries. Add a success criterion S12 whose evidence is a scenario that runs J14 after J7 and checks that each host clone passes git fsck with no romeu ref left and that every memory file parses as 03 3.9 without julieta. Add a guide page for it.
findings.cost: One journey, one criterion, one scenario function, one guide page.

findings.defect: retire moves a project to .attic inside the root and 'never deletes', and no command and no sentence anywhere tells the owner how to delete what they own (.attic, the state attic, salvage payloads); J13 step 4 is the only manual deletion, and it covers orphaned repo dirs only.
findings.scenario: Years of retired projects pile up under $ROMEU_ROOT/.attic with clones, salvage tarballs and transcripts; the owner wants them gone and finds no guidance on which directories are safe to remove or whether anything (doctor, status, the state attic) will complain afterwards.
findings.change: In 01 1.7 add to the retire row: 'what retire moves is the owner's; the owner deletes it by hand, as J7 step 4 says'. Add J7 step 4: once status shows nothing unpushed for the project, the operator may delete $ROMEU_ROOT/.attic/<name>/<ts>/ and $XDG_STATE_HOME/romeu/attic/<name>/<ts>/; romeu never does, and neither status nor doctor reads them afterwards. State in 04 4.2 that status and doctor tolerate their absence, and test it.
findings.cost: Two sentences, one journey step, one test that deletes an attic and runs status and doctor.

findings.defect: The no-delete rule binds the owner as well as the agent, and the accepted risk handles only a leaked credential ('rotate'); the value a user actually chooses, the project name, is kept forever in every entry's file name and project field and in every other sandbox's view, and a name cannot be rotated.
findings.scenario: A developer names a project after a client or an unannounced product; the contract ends and the client asks for removal; nothing in the spec lets the owner remove that project's entries, and a hand deletion leaves doctor failing on the view (04 4.2) with no documented recovery.
findings.change: In 13 13.5 add 'Owner removal': the rule binds romeu's code and agents; the operator may remove all entries of one project, or the whole ledger directory, by hand on the host, and the next ingest or doctor run derives the views again without reporting a failure. Name in the 05 5.4 secret row that a project name is the one user-chosen value the ledger keeps, and that the remedy for it is owner removal, not rotation. Record the distinction in ADR 0006 as a considered alternative (see L16-20).
findings.cost: A paragraph in 13 13.5, a row edit in 05 5.4, a doctor behaviour (derive the view again rather than fail when entries are gone) and its test; a maintainer decision, since the rule is the maintainer's.

findings.defect: A project created later under a retired project's name silently reads the retired project's ledger entries as its own, so data crosses from one owner or employer to another by name reuse.
findings.scenario: A developer retires 'api' from a past employer and later creates a personal 'api'; the new sandbox's own.jsonl lists the old employer's failures, tools and timings, and the new agent reads them as its own history.
findings.change: In 13 13.5 replace the sentence with a rule: sync of a project whose name has entries but no live or retired record refuses (exit 2, a new error id) unless the operator confirms on a TTY; or the generation-scoped view shows only entries ingested after the project record was created. Add a 13 13.10 row.
findings.cost: One rule, one error id, one test; choosing between the two options is a decision.

findings.defect: The trigger of 'finer visibility per project in the cross-project view', 'the first private project on a machine that also runs a public one', cannot be observed: the spec has no notion of a private or public project (03 3.2), and the row names no observer.
findings.scenario: A developer runs a work project and a personal project on one machine from day one; every agent on the machine reads the work project's name and activity times (13 13.6), and the event that should reopen the decision is never recognised, because nothing defines 'private'.
findings.change: Rewrite the trigger as observable: 'the operator syncs projects whose repo URLs belong to more than one GitHub owner or more than one gitHosts entry (romeu can see this at sync); or the operator says one project must not be seen, written as an issue. The maintainer observes the second.' Optionally have sync print a one-line notice the first time the first condition holds.
findings.cost: One table cell; optionally one notice and its test.

findings.defect: Salvage writes ignored files (.env, local keys, dumps) into ignored.tar.gz and, on request, transcripts with echoed tokens into the memory dir, which every later generation mounts read-write, which has no stated mode, which moves to .attic on retire and which machine backups take; the spec tells the user none of this.
findings.scenario: A recreate salvages a .env with production credentials; months later a new generation's agent, told to clean up old files, reads salvage/<old-gen>/ignored.tar.gz; another local account on a shared Mac reads the same file through a default umask of 022; Time Machine keeps it after the owner deletes it.
findings.change: In 08 8.5 add 'What salvage payloads hold': ignored.tar.gz and transcripts can hold secrets and the employer's code and prompts; they are written with mode 0600 in directories with mode 0700; they stay until the owner deletes them (L16-3); they are part of any backup of $ROMEU_ROOT. Have romeu salvage print that sentence once when it stores ignored files or transcripts. Either keep salvage/ of closed generations out of the sandbox's reach (moved outside the mounted memory dir after import) or list the read-write exposure as an accepted risk in 05 5.4 with the maintainer's decision.
findings.cost: A paragraph, two mode rules and their tests, one printed line; a decision on moving closed salvage out of the mount, which changes 02 2.3 and I24.

findings.defect: No mode is fixed for the host tree (memory, salvage payloads, spool, view, .attic, review checkouts); only settings, state and the ledger have one, and doctor checks only those.
findings.scenario: On a Mac with a second local account (a family account, a shared build user), memory entries, handoffs and salvage payloads under $HOME/dev are world-readable under the default umask.
findings.change: In 02 2.3 state that romeu creates <name>-env/, memory/, ledger/ and .attic/ with mode 0700 and julieta writes memory files with mode 0600; add a doctor row in 04 4.2 that fails on group- or world-readable bits under those directories; add the case to I12 or I24.
findings.cost: Two sentences, one doctor row, one test; a probe A3 check that sbx's direct mount keeps those modes as the sandbox sees them.

findings.defect: The mitigation of the memory-planting row is 'read memory only through romeu handoff', but that command shows only handoffs, so the owner is told not to open their own plain-file notes and is given no safe way to read memory entries on the host.
findings.scenario: A developer wants to read and keep the lessons the agent recorded for a repo; romeu handoff does not show them; following the guide, they never open the files; ignoring it, they open the directory in an editor, exactly the exposure the row describes.
findings.change: Add a host read command, romeu memory list|show <name> [--repo <dir>] [--json], through the os.Root readers of memstore with escaped output (I24, I29), and change the mitigation to 'read memory only through romeu handoff and romeu memory'. List the command in 00 0.5 as needed by the owner's read path.
findings.cost: One read-only command, its reference page, an I24/I29 test and a scenario line.

findings.defect: Through the tool, only the agent can delete a memory entry (julieta memory rm, Store.Delete), with no history (I24 forbids .git) and no copy in salvage, and the threat model does not mention memory among the work an agent may destroy.
findings.scenario: An agent decides that ten old entries are stale and removes them; the owner's months of notes on the repo are gone with no trace, and no salvage, snapshot or residual-risk row covers it.
findings.change: In 08 8.1 either keep deleted entries (memory rm moves an entry to a dated file under entries/ marked status: deleted, or a trash under the allowlist) or add a 05 5.4 row: 'an agent can delete memory entries; nothing keeps them', with the maintainer's acceptance. Whichever is chosen, say in 08 8.1 that backups of memory are the owner's responsibility.
findings.cost: Either a small change to the store and a test, or a residual-risk row and a decision.

findings.defect: The workload's per-name volumes 'reattach on recreate', so they outlive rm and recreate, yet the spec never treats them as a store: it does not say what they hold, whether rm or retire removes them, or how the owner removes them.
findings.scenario: A developer retires a project and believes it is gone from the sandbox side; the volume with the agent's home, caches and possibly login credentials stays in sbx and comes back into a later sandbox that has the same name.
findings.change: Add to block A (11 11.1, A6 or A12) an observation of which volumes the workload declares and what survives sbx env rm; add the volumes to the store table (L16-1); say in 04 4.2 what rm and retire do with them (left in place, reported by status) and in J14 how to remove them.
findings.cost: One probe observation, one table row, one status line, one journey step.

findings.defect: The redaction rule removes only home path, user name, host name and root path, while block A records the maintainer's real host global git config (A1) and sbx global rules and secrets (A9) into a public repository, where emails, internal hosts in url.insteadOf, and an employer's domains or service names would be published.

findings.change: Extend the Redaction row of 10 10.3 with the positive scrub that plan.md question 8 proposes: real values only for the harness's own sandboxes and env dirs, typed placeholders for every other row of a listing, typed parsers for git config, trust settings and key listings, and a unit test planting an email, an internal host and a foreign global rule.
findings.cost: One table cell and the recorder work the plan already proposes.

findings.defect: Memory has an import format (JSONL) and a verify command but no export, so moving memory to another machine or another tool has no defined round trip, and J12 says only that memory is machine-local.

postmortem: After v1.0.0 the tool kept its promise that nothing sandbox-only was lost, and that is how it failed. (1) Nobody could say what it held: an employer review asked where its code, secrets and transcripts were, and the answer was spread over seven sections and three trees plus sbx volumes (index S1-S11, 01 1.1, 01 1.2, 02 2.3, 02 2.4, 06 6.2, 13 13.1). (2) Leaving was not a journey: users deleted $HOME/dev whole and lost memory, or left everything behind forever (09, 12 12.8, ADR 0001 rule 12, 00 0.3). (3) The notes were plain files the user was told not to open, and the sanctioned reader shows no entries (05 5.4, 01 1.3 D, 04 4.2, 08 8.1). (4) The agent could delete notes and the owner could not (04 4.3, I24, 08 8.1, index Boundaries). (5) Secrets lived forever in ignored.tar.gz and transcripts, readable by later sandboxes, other local accounts and backups (08 8.5, 02 2.3, 04 4.2, 05 5.4). (6) 'Never deleted' met a client's deletion request, and a hand deletion made doctor fail (13, 13 13.5, ADR 0006, 05 5.4). (7) Project names crossed boundaries: every sandbox read every name, and a reused name inherited a retired project's events (13 13.5, 13 13.6, 05 5.4, index Deferred decisions). (8) One machine, one root, one ledger, with the override reserved for tests (02 2.4, 13 13.1). (9) Knowledge left with the person: memory is machine-local and outside the repo (00 0.6, 08 8.1, Q14, J12). (10) Unsaid: the spec is written by and for one maintainer who is also the only user and trusts himself as the host; every data rule is a rule against the agent, and the owner as a person with rights over their data, and the employer as a second owner, have no seat in the threat model, the success criteria or the users table; the index has 36 deferred rows and not one of them is about them (05 threat model, 00 0.2, index Deferred decisions).
lens_critique: The lens imports a multi-party data governance frame (an employer, deletion requests, other local users) into a v1 that serves one developer, who is owner, operator and maintainer at once, on his own Mac, with nothing sent off the machine. For that user 'nothing is lost' really is the success that matters, and every deletion path is a new way to lose work. Read strictly, the lens would push mechanisms (purge commands, per-project visibility, multi-instance roots) ahead of their last responsible moment. Most of its value here is in words, not mechanisms: an inventory, a leaving journey, modes and one sentence that says nothing leaves. The lens also undervalues what the spec already does well: no free text in events, plain-file formats with CC0 schemas, and plain clones instead of submodules.
missing_viewpoint: The organization's IT or compliance administrator who decides whether the tool may run on a managed Mac at all (MDM and org policy over sbx, GPL-3.0-only licensing, approved egress, audit needs): no lens judges installability and policy fit from the organization's side, apart from the person whose data it is.

confidence: High on the absences (checked with a search over the spec for export, delete, uninstall, retention, mode and backup); medium on the severity calls, since the primary user is also the maintainer and may accept several of these as they are.
